questions.topic: The growing population of the elderly
questions.learningObjective: Argue why faster elderly growth strained the Social Security system
questions.stem: Ticket OPS-1061 asks the documentation crew to argue, for a briefing note, why faster growth in the elderly population strained the Social Security system during the 1970s.

answer.exemplar: Social Security paid benefits mainly from payroll taxes collected on workers. When the number of beneficiaries rose faster than the number of covered workers, the trust fund drew down faster than it was replenished. The baby-boom cohort reaching sixty-five in the 1970s added beneficiaries while the labor force grew more slowly, so lawmakers faced the choice of higher taxes, lower benefits, or a larger trust fund.

questions.explanation: Payroll taxes fund benefits, so the balance depends on workers and beneficiaries. When the elderly grew faster than covered workers, the ratio worsened and pressure for tax or benefit changes mounted.
questions.hint: Ask who pays and who receives.

answer.exemplar: Before reliable contraception, many women completed school and entered marriage and childbearing in quick sequence. answer.exemplar: A family leaving the hospital with a parent who could no longer manage at home met a gap between two benefit systems. Medicare paid for the hospital stay and a short skilled-nursing benefit, then stopped. Custodial care in a nursing home, or care at home by relatives, was not covered. questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Lowering the voting age
questions.learningObjective: Describe what states had to change after the voting-age amendment
questions.stem: Ticket OPS-1078 asks the documentation crew to describe, for a civics handbook, what states had to change once the voting age moved to eighteen everywhere.

answer.exemplar: The amendment applied to federal, state, and local elections, so state legislatures had to amend their own voting statutes, change registration forms, adjust ballot and equipment rules for the newly eligible, and train local officials. Several states had already lowered their ages, so their work was limited, while states that kept twenty-one faced the larger task. Because state and local offices administered elections, the change could not take effect on election day alone.

questions.explanation: Election administration sat with states and counties, so the amendment required changes to statutes, forms, equipment, and training. States that had already lowered their ages faced little work.
questions.hint: Remember who runs elections locally.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Paying for the care of the elderly
questions.learningObjective: Identify the coverage gap described in congressional testimony

stimulus.body: Our residents stay with us for years, not weeks. The federal program pays for a limited period of skilled nursing after a hospital stay and for nothing at all beyond that. The care that fills the rest of these residents' lives is not paid for by anyone.

questions.stem: Ticket VOTE-077 attaches this testimony to the coverage file. Which gap does it expose?

options.text: The payment covered hospital care but stopped at the hospital door for every beneficiary
options.misconception: Overstates the end of coverage at discharge

options.text: The payment covered custodial care fully but left hospital admissions underfunded
options.misconception: Reverses which setting was underfunded

options.text: The payment covered acute and short skilled-nursing care but not the custodial long-term care residents needed
The payment was adequate for nursing care but weak on transportation to the hospital
options.misconception: Invents a transportation gap the testimony never mentions

questions.explanation: The testimony marks the boundary between covered medical care and uncovered custodial long-term care. Coverage did not end at every hospital door, and transportation is not the issue.
questions.hint: Look for the boundary in the payment rules.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The growing population of the elderly
questions.learningObjective: Weigh beneficiary counts and per-person costs in program spending growth
questions.stem: Ticket POL-315 asks the policy team to weigh two accounts of why federal spending on programs for the elderly grew faster than the elderly population itself in the 1970s.

options.text: Neither explains it, since federal spending on the elderly was flat across the decade
options.misconception: Describes spending that never grew

options.text: Only the number of beneficiaries matters, since per-person costs never rose in the period
options.misconception: Assumes per-person costs stayed flat through the 1970s

options.text: Only costs per person matter, since the number of beneficiaries stayed constant
options.misconception: Ignores the growth in the number of beneficiaries

options.text: Both: more beneficiaries and higher per-person medical costs pushed spending up faster than head counts

questions.explanation: Program spending grew faster than the elderly population because both the number of beneficiaries and per-person medical costs rose. Either factor alone understates the increase.
questions.hint: Count beneficiaries and cost per beneficiary.
